title: Awakening in A Female Form
speaker: Zenshin Florence Caplow and Jean LaValley
summary: Zenshin Florence Caplow and Jean LaValley tell the stories of awakened women from the Therigatha and from Chinese, Japanese, and Theravada traditions, opening a weekend on women's koans. Zenshin recounts Mahapajapati leading shaven-headed women to ask the Buddha for ordination, Soma sending Mara away, and Rionan burning her face to be accepted as a student. Jean describes arriving at koans from Vipassana, asks why gender goes unmentioned in the Dharma hall, and reads the story of Chiyono, a servant whose bucket loses its bottom. The evening closes with Dipa Ma taking a frightened student's hand on a turbulent flight and saying, "The daughters of Buddha are fearless."

Speaker labels mark the handovers the recording makes clear.
In some stretches the recording does not show which of them is speaking, so those passages carry no new label.]*

**Zenshin Florence Caplow:** But what really hasn't changed, and this is what I have been learning as I've been doing my own study on this subject, is the desire to wake up, the desire to understand what it is to be a human being, what it is to be in this world, what the universe is.
This has been shared by men and women throughout history.
The circumstances change, but the heart of awakening has always been there for both men and women.
And yet, oddly enough, we really only know the male voices generally in connection with this heart of awakening.
The women's voices have been lost, or hidden, or forgotten.
And really, that has a lot to do with this way that it's been so different to be a woman than to be a man for so much of the history.
In Asia, and still in many places in Asia, being a woman is just so completely different than being male.
And I'm actually quoting here: *women were seen as weak, cowardly, spiteful, sexually aggressive*, which is really interesting.
It actually turns out that that was a common feeling about women, that they were the sexual aggressors, and that men needed to be sort of protected from them.

And so, bound by the difficulties of being female, you think about the dangers of birth for most of human history, the control of fathers, brothers, sons, the vulnerability to rape and violence, it makes sense that people might think of being born as a woman as actually karmic retribution for past unskillful action, because it was so hard to be a woman in comparison with being a man.
And it was said, and is still believed in some places, that women are seven lifetimes behind men on the path of awakening, and that the only way to fully awaken, to be a Buddha, is in a man's body.
And I do think when you think about women's lives, it makes some sense, because the barriers for women were so strong.
Yet one of the great gifts of Buddhist teaching is the teaching of non-duality, of non-self.
And in that view, there is no male, and there is no female.

So right along with this whole difficulty of being female, there is this great teaching: our true nature, the true nature of reality, is so vast and so unbounded that it isn't even touched by our ideas of what's possible for us as a man or a woman.
And this is powerfully liberating.
But it's also tricky, because in this great vast view, it's true that there is neither male nor female, and yet we live in this relative world where being male and female really matters.
I recently came across the story of the vow of Tara.
I think most of you know that Tara is the female embodiment of enlightenment and deeply beloved by the Tibetan peoples.
I'd never heard the story of her vow, but it's really wonderful.
Tara was once the princess Wisdom Moon, and she was deeply devoted to the Dharma and tremendously wise.
A monk came to her and said what a shame it was that she would have to come back as a man before being enlightened.
And this is what the princess said in response to the monk's concern for her:
*Here there is no man, no woman, no self, no person and no consciousness.
Labeling male or female is hollow.
Oh, how worldly fools delude themselves.*
This is a perfect example of teaching from the absolute.
This is completely true.
She's speaking the truth here.
But then she says:
*Those who wish to attain supreme enlightenment in the form of a man are many, but those who wish to serve the aims of beings in a woman's body are few.
Therefore may I, until this world is emptied out, until everyone is enlightened, work for the benefit of sentient beings in a woman's body.*
So at this point, she completely expresses compassion from the relative view.
She's holding both.

Although I have been a serious Buddhist practitioner for 25 years, it's only recently that I really noticed that I was only hearing male voices and that I didn't know the teachings and stories of women.
The first person who really woke me up to this is a wonderful Zen teacher, Joan Sutherland.
One of the things she was doing back maybe about 10 years ago was actually beginning to collect these stories.
I had a chance to practice with her around some of these, and it was an eye-opening experience.
I was hoping she was going to do a book, but she never got around to doing a book.
So about a year ago, I started collecting them myself.
I found more and more in the process of looking through books and translations and obscure references.
I began to get really excited, because the women that I was discovering and the stories I was discovering were absolutely extraordinary.
I want to just point out one of the images back here.
So, this image behind Jean of the bristlecone pine: some of you may know these trees or may have seen them in your life if you're lucky.
They're the oldest trees on earth.
Some of the living trees are over 5,000 years old.
They grow up above 10,000 feet in the desert mountains in Eastern California and Nevada, in basically desert environments where nothing else can grow.
And yet because of that environment, because of those difficulties, they are some of the most beautiful trees on earth.

I feel like that's what I've seen from encountering these women and these stories: the very barriers that they faced make their practice completely inspiring for both men and women, to realize that in the face of everything that kept them from awakening, they really didn't let anything stop them.
And they grew into these utterly unique forms.
So that's why I put that up there, to remind us, because all of us face things in our lives.
And we can all be like the bristlecone pines, unique and beautiful.
The other thing I began to realize is it really matters when we don't know these things.
Norman Fischer tells a story about when he was abbot at San Francisco Zen Center.
All over the world at Zen Centers, for centuries, people have chanted the male lineage, the lineage of teacher, student, from the Buddha to you.
The Zen Center at San Francisco had been doing that as well, and nobody had really given too much thought to the fact that they were all male names.
That was what had happened.
It had been one man and another and another and another, and finally Suzuki Roshi and the rest of us.
But a woman came to Norman in an interview, a young woman, and she began to cry.
And she said, "Every time I hear those names, and there's not a single woman's name, I feel that I don't have a right to be in this meditation hall."
And he got it.
He describes it as like an arrow going into his heart.
He felt her pain.
And on that day he started, and it's not easy to get things done at San Francisco Zen Center, even if you're the abbot, he started working to have a women's lineage chanted.
I just have to say he was successful.

And just this fall, the Soto Zen Buddhist Association, the national association, agreed that they would encourage the centers all over the country to chant a women's lineage, and we will be chanting one this weekend.
I just want to say a little bit about where some of these stories come from.
You'll be hearing a lot of them tonight and over the weekend.
The earliest ones come from the Therigatha, which is a collection of stories and poems written down about the original women disciples of the Buddha.
And they're beautiful.
They're all the nuns that practiced with the Buddha.
Many of them are from the Koan literature of China, Japan, Korea.
I want to say a little bit about Koans, because I know Jean is going to address this a bit too.
There are a lot of misunderstandings, I think, about Koans, and maybe even a little fear of them.
Koans actually started as stories from individual great teachers.
There'd be some wonderful teacher, and his or her students would write down lectures that they gave, but also dialogues that they had, maybe with their teacher, with other peers, with their students.
They'd be called the record of so and so.
Over time, many of these dialogues had these great turning moments where somebody had a moment of deep understanding.
People started collecting these dialogues because they realized that, though they're very short, they contained the seed or heart of practice.
And over time, a whole way of working with them developed, where sometimes a student would take that dialogue and really take it into their life and practice.
Or they'd take a phrase or even just a single word.
That's a whole form of Zen practice.
The Rinzai school is famous for working with these stories in that way.
In a way, it's taking somebody else's awakening, or expression of awakening, and it becomes a candle that can awaken your own understanding.
I'm not trained in this way and we won't be doing that this weekend.
But we are going to be working with these Koans, and we can take their spirit of questioning and playfulness into our lives.
Koans are also sometimes called the family stories of Zen, and that's more how in Soto Zen we work with them.
These are the stories of our ancestors.
The only thing is that for most of us in the Zen tradition, we know these family stories, but we only know the stories of our great uncles and our great, great grandfathers.
It's as if we had the family stories and we never had the stories of our grandmothers or our great aunts.
So knowing these stories, as I've begun to learn them, is like learning the stories of a whole side of my family that I never knew.
With that, let me just say one other thing.
One way to understand Koans too is that they can be the inspiration to look at the question, or Koan, that arises from your own life, from your own circumstances.
Each person here in this room carries a spiritual question, at least one, if not a hundred.
And part of what we'll be doing this weekend is helping, hopefully, for those questions to come forward in your life.
So with that, we turn it over to Jean for a little bit.
In our notes, it says, "Over to you, Jean."
Little did we know that literally it would be over to you with this thing.
**Jean LaValley:** Okay.
So probably nine months ago, Florence and I were practicing together, because we practice together every year.
We begin our practice with a day of talking, and then we go into silence for a while, and then we end our time together with a lot more talking.
She started telling me about her project, and we started talking, and this idea that we could explore this together came up.
I want to tell you a little bit about what's happened to me as I've worked with this, and with Florence, over the last six or eight months.
The only form of Buddhism that I've ever practiced is in the Theravada tradition, which is called insight or Vipassana in this country.
I knew nothing about koans.

My very limited understanding was that they were really, really, really, really hard questions with only one right answer, and that they were given to you by very stern monks who gave you no help at all.
Now, as a competitive and rather insecure person, this did not sound like something I wanted to take on.
It seemed like a very hard test, and I didn't want to fail.
But it was Florence, and I've always been energized by my Dharma sisters' rigor and determination and investigation.
So fairly early on, Florence and I agreed on a name for this weekend, which came to be freedom in a female form, exploring the stories and koans of awakened women.
Now, that is a lot of words and a lot of concepts.
So early on, I decided, well, I'm not going to focus on freedom, what that is.
It's been said that asking people to describe enlightenment is like having deaf people describe Mozart.
And I did not want to express my deafness in public, so I didn't want to go there.
Then I found a lovely definition by Stephen Batchelor about enlightenment and awakening:
*The Buddha's awakening is not about some privileged state of mind or the unconditioned state, but rather about a complex of truths.
She or he awakens to a way of understanding the world and then a way of behaving in the world.*
I just thought that was a beautiful, useful definition.
Someone had done a really good job.
I could move on.
So I breathed with all the other words in this every day, trying to see, as Florence suggested, what arose for me.
And as I worked with this, I realized I had an ever-growing series of questions that started to take on a certain direction.
So I'm going to read them.
I sort of compiled them.
Is freedom different for women?
Are the experiences that lead to freedom different for men and women?
How does being in a female form affect our spiritual work?
How much of what I think we think is hormonally driven?
Testosterone versus estrogen.
Should we embrace this difference, overcome this difference, or maybe just ignore this difference?
What are the possibilities and dangers of embracing femaleness?
And lastly, practitioners are often encouraged to think of others before considering themselves, which is a variant of "you do not practice for yourself, you practice for all sentient beings."
But we wondered, is that instruction geared for men who may think of themselves first?
Because women tend to live their lives putting others first.
I mean, as one woman said in a group that Florence was in, "I always put others first.
That's my problem."
So these began to seem like pretty provocative questions, going in a direction that I didn't expect, because they all seem to be gender based.
And as Florence said in her opening, I'm going to ask you to do something that we don't do very much in a meditation hall, which is to really consider gender.
So it seemed like whether I planned on thinking about gender or not, I was going to be working with gender.
And gender always seems like the elephant in the Buddhist Dharma hall.
I mean, we all know it's there, but we rarely mention it, or we talk around it.
So why don't we talk about this?
I thought about that a lot.
But before I could really delve into that question, another question arose, which was, who are you to be asking these questions?
Yeah, we have some thoughts on that, too.
You're wondering that yourself.
This is Mara speaking.
Who are you to be asking, you know, is it okay to investigate elephants?
I mean, is the fact that I'm even wondering about this the sign that I'm such a deluded practitioner because it seemed like it was bothering that many other people.
When I was a practicing Catholic, I knew that my job was to learn what was in the Baltimore Catechism, and when in doubt, believe the Pope.
That didn't work very well for me, and so I stopped being a Catholic.
So I thought about Buddhism.
One of the really inviting aspects of Buddhism, I think, and I think many of us do, is that one is really encouraged to see for oneself.
There's a Pali word, ehipassiko, which means come and see.
It's really saying the Dharma welcomes all investigation, the Dharma welcomes being put to the test.
With this in mind, I reread the Kalama Sutta, which [unclear: "I don't send people"].
Sure.
Okay.

The Kalamas were a group of people who lived at the time of the Buddha, and at the time of the Buddha many people were wandering around saying, "This is the truth, this is the truth, this is the truth."
The question the Kalamas asked the Buddha was, "Well, how do we know what is true?"
As I thought about my question, what is the place of gender in all of this, I thought, I need some guidelines.
So I reread the Kalama Sutta, which is in the Anguttara Nikaya, part of the canon.
I'm going to quote one paragraph.

*Come, Kalamas, do not go upon what has been acquired by repeated hearing, nor upon tradition, nor upon scripture, nor upon surmise, nor upon axiom, nor upon specious reasoning, nor upon bias towards a notion that has been pondered over, nor upon another's seeming ability, nor upon the consideration, "The monk is our teacher."
When you yourselves know these things are bad, blamable, censured by the wise, undertaken and observed, these things lead to harm and ill, abandon them.
When you yourselves know these things are good, blameless, praised by the wise, undertaken and observed, these things lead to happiness and benefit, enter on and abide in them.*
Now, this passage is not the Buddhist carte blanche for, "Well, see what feels right, and just believe that."
But the Buddha is saying, when you know these things lead to benefit and happiness, that's worth paying attention to, and when we know these things lead to harm, they are not good things.
The ability to question and then test one's beliefs in an appropriate way is called appropriate attention.
The ability to recognize and choose wise people to give you feedback, not a phrase the Buddha probably used, is called admirable friends.

These two pillars, appropriate attention and admirable friends, are pillars that I consciously have been trying to apply, and we're going to be applying them this weekend because they will serve us well.
So I felt pretty grounded in who am I to ask this question.
It seemed like a perfectly good question to ask.
Then I came back to this whole question: why did it take so long to even have the gender elephant actually wave its trunk in the Dharma Hall or whatever?
That's not in the talk.
I just made that up.
This is why I think this question hasn't been raised in the way Florence and I are raising it.
First of all, this whole general approach of ehipassiko, come and see, is so invigorating and produces such positive momentum that I think it's really easy to practice on that stream of momentum.
That's a good thing.
There's so much to investigate: Nicha, Dukkha, Anatta.
It's easy to do that without a gender lens.
It's a very compelling practice, and I think it's fairly easy to ignore the gender piece of it.
Another aspect, I think, of why I haven't, and maybe we haven't addressed this, is that often when the question of gender arises, anger arises.
As a good Buddhist, I know that anger is not the right thing, or at least rage isn't the right thing.
I have to say that when gender arose, I was often rageful, and so it was a lot easier to say, "Well, let's just focus on something else."
I would briefly acknowledge it, notice, notice, notice, rage, rage, rage, and then I would pledge to rise above.
The strongest reason, I think, that we ignore gender is what Florence has already mentioned: that enlightened beings don't see male or female.
So the implication is that there's no need to spend any time on the gender thing, because the trouble will go away once we are enlightened.
This is probably true, and it makes sense.
But my reality is that there is gender, and that gender creates a lot of conditions in my world.
Then I started to think about it.
The enlightened mind, by report, is neither self nor not self.
And yet we actually spend quite a lot of practice time deconstructing a sense of self.
We're taking it apart and looking at the pieces and seeing how we put it together.
That's really useful.
We get a lot of training in deconstructing the self.
Now, I think most of you know that many Theravadan teachers are psychotherapists, and they're very clear in saying that you have to understand the self before you can let that self go.
So on the self side, there seems to be a lot of interest in deconstructing something that's apparently going to disappear when we're enlightened.
But I could find really no parallel instruction about gender.
Rita Gross is a Buddhist practitioner, but she teaches women in religion, actually in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, which, I'm from Wisconsin, I know this is not a prestigious thing.
But I really just want to go and spend a winter with her.
Anyhow, I'm sorry, that was a little digression.
She says:
*Be useful to contemplate gender as a component made out of biology, cultural expectations, and habitual patterns, rather than anything that exists truly and substantially.
It is useful to deconstruct every other thing that seems to be an entity into its component parts.
Now that transformation takes a great deal of time and effort.
And just as training is necessary for people to actually approach egolessness, so training is required to transcend the prison of gender roles.*
End quote.
In the last six months, I've become quite clear, not mad, just clear, that the gender issue is not about politics and power.
It really is at heart a practice question, and ignoring gender is not a useful practice approach.
It's not uncommon for women to try to talk to a teacher about these issues, or about how men and women are different, or how it feels to be female, or anything like that.
And it's really not uncommon for the teacher to say, "No male, no female, there's no value in considering these things," and tell us to go back to the cushion.
Just a little heads up here: this weekend, we will be considering those things.
I said that one of the things to pay attention to as you read the Koans is what arises for you.
I think that my little bio here can tell you that what arises can be very surprising, and I have to say, really fascinating.
So that's one woman's report from the field about what can happen with Koan study.
So why don't you tell us some stories?
**Zenshin Florence Caplow:** So she's right.
That's exactly what I'm going to do.
I'm going to tell stories now.
I want you to imagine that we're all sitting around the fire together on a cold winter's night, and you're going to hear stories of your grannies and aunties.
This is just the beginning.
I'd like to start with the oldest granny of all in our tradition.
How many people here in this room know who Mahapajapati was?
Okay, well, you're about to learn about her.
Mahapajapati was the Buddha's foster mother and his aunt.
His mother died just a few days after he was born.

She raised the Buddha, and then he went off and had his great enlightenment, and he came back a few years later, and his teachings were so powerful that many of the men of the Sakyan clan immediately abandoned their families and became monks.
So there were all these women who no longer had their husbands, no longer had their sons, no longer had their fathers.
And again, in this culture, those things were the woman's protection.
Those were the woman's life.
Then there was a war.
I think maybe with the Koliyas.
I can't remember, anyway.
There was another war.
Many more men died, so there were more women who were widowed and alone.
They began to come to Mahapajapati because she was very wise and kind to these women.
They came to her for comfort and for teaching.
Eventually there were so many women that she decided she would go to the Buddha and ask if women could be ordained, because at this point the Sangha was entirely male.
So she went to the Buddha and she asked, and the Buddha said no.
She asked three times, and the Buddha said, "Do not set your heart on this."
No.
This might have deterred a less determined and wise woman.
This did not deter Mahapajapati.
She went home.
She thought about it for a little while.
She gathered these women to her.
They shaved their own heads.
They cut off their hair.
They put on the robes of monks, and they walked hundreds of miles to where the Buddha was teaching at the time.
So this huge group of women arrives outside the walls of the city where the Buddha is teaching.
They're the former court ladies of the Buddha's kingdom, and they're muddy and dirty and sweaty and scratched, and don't have any hair.
They set up a wailing outside the walls, it's said.
Ananda, the Buddha's attendant and his cousin and probably a relative of many of these women, comes out and asks what's happening.
Mahapajapati explains to him that they have come to be ordained by the Buddha.
So Ananda intercedes, and he goes to the Buddha and asks if women can join the holy life.
The Buddha says no again.
Ananda asked three times, and the Buddha says no three times.
Ananda then takes another tack.
He says, "Well, most esteemed one, can women achieve the same enlightenment that men can?"
It's very clear in all the versions of the story that the Buddha says yes, they can.

So Ananda says, "Well, if women can attain the same enlightenment as men, and given that you might not even be alive if Mahapajapati had not suckled you at her own breasts, perhaps you should allow them to ordain."
And the Buddha says yes.
So Mahapajapati was the first woman to be ordained.
The story goes there were 500, but that just means very many in that realm.
Many women were then ordained after her.
That was the beginning of what became the four noble groups, which were monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen practitioners.
So now you know the story of your oldest granny.
As I said, the Terigata is the collection of these nuns' stories, and they're really quite wonderful.
Here's one of my favorites.
This is the story of Soma and Mara.
I was teasing Jean about Mara earlier.
Mara is the embodiment of delusion.
He's the closest thing in Buddhist practice that there is to the devil, and he did a lot of tempting of the Buddha as well on the night of his enlightenment.
So Soma is in good company here.
Soma was a nun, and she was sitting by herself in the forest under a tree, deep in meditation practice, when Mara arrives invisibly, it's said, and whispers in her ear.
This is what he whispers: "Women's consciousness is naturally limited, and wisdom is very difficult to attain.
So by what right do you practice?"
And she says, "The desire for awakening, can it possibly be limited by a woman's consciousness?
Am I a man in this respect or a woman?
Mara, be gone."
And Mara disappears.
I think we can all take Soma as our own, whether we're male or female.
There's always that little whisper of, "Do you have a right?"
It just happens that for women there's a twist on it.
Anyway, I love that.
Mara, be gone.
There's actually a long gap between the Terigata and any other stories of women.
As many of you may know, the lineage of nuns died out in India, and in fact it died out across much of Asia.
Many of even the women who practice as nuns now do not practice with full ordination, because the ordination lineage died.
You can kind of see why: when women are seen as less valuable, and you get less merit by supporting them, you don't support your nuns.
Where you do start to hear the stories of women again is starting in about the seventh or eighth century in China, when Buddhism and Chan begin to develop.
What had been there for more than a thousand years before was Confucianism, and Confucianism is quite clear about the positions of men and women.

In Confucian belief, the subordination of women to their fathers, husbands and sons, in that order, is considered actually the natural way of the universe, and to disturb that is to disturb the structure of the universe.

What that meant is that for a woman to want to engage in deep practice, to ordain or to study in a monastery, she actually had to have the permission of her family, the permission of the male members of her family.
Some women waited an entire lifetime, and probably beyond, for that permission.
But enough women did receive that permission, or found ways of practicing as laywomen, that we have wonderful, amazing stories of women from China.

In fact, many of you who are Zen students may not know that Bodhidharma, the semi-mythological ancestor of Zen practitioners in China, had four primary disciples, and one of them was a woman, a nun whose name was Zongqi.
And we don't know anything really about her beyond that, but we do know that she was one of his primary students.

One of the things that's quite interesting about these Chinese stories (there's a lot of humor actually in Chinese Zen) is that many, many of the stories of women in China involve encounters between very ordinary women, not great teachers necessarily, but women who were working in the fields or women who run tea shops on the side of the road.
They have some encounter with a famous master, and the woman comes out on top in the encounter in some way.
She teaches the master something that he couldn't see within his world, his monastic, carefully controlled world.
So I'm going to tell you a few of these.
One of my favorites is called Miao Zong's Dharma interview.
This is one of the more well-known ones, actually.
Some of you may have heard it before.
Miao Zong later (that's actually her ordained name) became a very famous women's Zen teacher.
But at this time she was a lay woman, a very strong practitioner.
She would go to the monastery of Daohui, one of our great Zen ancestors, and practice with him.
When she came, she would stay in the abbot's quarters, which were like the guest quarters, the place for the honored guests.
And the head monk of the monastery made, as they say in the story, disapproving noises.
Always made disapproving noises.
There's a suggestion that maybe he thought Daohui was fooling around with her, or maybe he thought that she didn't deserve to be treated so.
Not only was she not ordained, she was a woman.
So he makes these noises, and apparently Daohui finally gets tired of it and says, "I think you should go talk to her yourself."
He reluctantly agrees.
He goes with his attendance to her doorway, and he knocks on her door, rings the bell or whatever it is that he does.
She comes to the door and he says, "I would like to meet with you."
She says, "Will this be a Dharma interview or a worldly interview?"
And he says, with great presence and pompousness, "A Dharma interview.
Of course, I'm a monk."
So she says, "Well, then dismiss your attendance and come back."
He dismisses his attendance and walks into her room, and she's lying face up on the bed, stark naked.
So this is her Dharma interview with a monk.
He points at her genitals and says, "What is that?"
And she says, "This is the doorway through which all the Buddhas and all the great teachers and all the monks have come into the world."
And he has nothing to say.
She says, "The Dharma interview is over," and turns her back to him.
There's a little postscript to this where he goes back to his teacher and he's very ashamed.
The teacher says something like, "Yeah, that old beast knows a little, doesn't she?"
So anyway, that's the story of Miao Tseung.
This Miao Tseung one is really not in this category, but there are literally dozens of wise old woman or tea lady stories.
I can't even believe how many I'm finding.
I'm really fascinated by this because these women would have been so unimportant culturally.
It actually says something about Zen that it recognized the wisdom in ordinary people, in seemingly unimportant people.
And maybe in fact their very unimportance enabled them to see something that the monks couldn't see.
I'll tell you one more.
I love this one.
It's called the old woman's miraculous powers.
Often the women are not named, although it turns out that in Koans many people are not named, so they're not alone in that.
In this one, Nanquan, Magu, and another monk were on pilgrimage.
I think they were young monks; that's my sense in the story.
They're going to go see a famous master, and they're walking along the road and they meet this old woman, who invites them in for a cup of tea.
Very sweet.
So they come in for their cup of tea and she sets out three cups.
She brings in the pot of tea and then she says, "Please show me your miraculous powers by drinking how you will drink a cup of tea with your miraculous powers."
The three monks just look at each other.
They're completely nonplussed.
They have no idea what to do.
So she says, "Well, this decrepit old woman will show you her miraculous powers."
She picks up the pot of tea, pours three cups of tea, puts the pot down, and leaves the room.
She demonstrates her miraculous powers, which is what miraculous spiritual powers are: ordinary lives, ordinary actions.
She shows them that miraculous powers are not lights in the sky.
They're pouring a cup of tea.
There are also stories, and I'm quite moved by these actually, of men going to women for teaching.
Here's one from seventeenth-century China, called Zhirong's ship of compassion.
Zhirong was a woman who was recognized by the emperor as a great teacher, and he gave her the name ship of compassion, which is just beautiful.
